title: BCA Investigation: Final Report
location: Bureau of Civic Accountability Headquarters — Ashenmere

narrative.text: Maren Tovik's investigation boards now cover every wall of her office, and the lines between names have formed a dense web that, from a distance, resembles a nervous system. She has been working on this for nearly two years. Today is the day she tells you what she has found — all of it, without reservation, without the careful qualifications that marked her earlier reports. Vyktor Reznik is present, at your request. He stands near the door, his expression unreadable.

Chancellor. The investigation is complete. I will present the findings in three categories: Halvek-era crimes, transition-period corruption, and — this is the category I did not anticipate when we began — current administration. I will begin with the third category, because it is the one that concerns you most directly. The BCA has investigated seventeen individuals currently serving in your government or closely associated with it. Of those seventeen, we have found sufficient evidence to recommend prosecution of six. Four cases involve procurement fraud — steering government contracts to family members or business associates. One involves the acceptance of bribes from a Lytheiran construction consortium. The sixth involves the destruction of evidence related to BNI-era crimes — not commission of those crimes, but active concealment of them after the transition.
She pauses. The pause is different this time — heavier. Vyktor shifts his weight near the door.

The sixth case is Vyktor Reznik. Your Chief of Staff. The investigation has established that between 1961 and 1963 — during the transition period — Vyktor personally authorized the destruction of seventeen boxes of BNI operational records. These records documented interrogation protocols, informant networks, and the identities of BNI operatives who participated in the torture of political prisoners. Vyktor's stated reason at the time was that the records were a 'security risk' — that making them public would trigger reprisals against former BNI personnel and destabilize the transition. The legal question is whether this constitutes obstruction of justice. The political question is whether your government can prosecute its own Chief of Staff for covering up crimes that predate the transition. I am presenting the legal case. The political question is yours.
Vyktor does not move. He does not look at you. He looks at the wall — at the investigation boards, at the lines connecting names to names, at his own name somewhere in the web he helped you build.

She is correct. I destroyed the records. I did it in February of 1963 — two months before the election. The records named forty-three Veltrians who had informed on their neighbors, their colleagues, their families. If those names had become public, some of those people would have been killed. Others would have killed the people who informed on them. I made a judgment. I did not consult anyone because I knew that consulting anyone would make them complicit in a decision that should have been mine alone. I am not asking for forgiveness. I am informing you of what happened and why.

Vyktor. The man who has been at my side since the day I took this office. The man who briefed me every morning, who told me truths I did not want to hear, who made himself indispensable to a government he was not sure would survive. He destroyed evidence. He covered up the names of informants — and some of those informants were probably torturers. He made a choice in the chaos of the transition, alone in a records room, deciding what history would remember and what it would forget. And now Maren Tovik is asking me to decide whether that choice was a crime — and whether I am willing to prosecute the man who has been the most indispensable person in my government.

choices.text: "Prosecute him. Maren, build your case — the same standard of evidence, the same standard of law, the same standard of accountability that applies to everyone else your investigation has identified. Vyktor, I am not going to stand here and tell you that I am sorry. You destroyed evidence. You made a choice about what the country was allowed to know about its own past, and you made that choice alone, in secret, without authorization from anyone. That is not how democracy works. That is how the old regime worked — decisions made in private by people who decided they knew better than everyone else. I have trusted you with more than I have trusted anyone in this government. That trust does not exempt you from the law. It cannot. That is the whole point."

"Vyktor, you will resign. Today. You will issue a public statement acknowledging that you destroyed records during the transition, explaining your reasoning, and accepting that your actions — whatever their motivation — were incompatible with the standards this government requires. Maren, you will not prosecute. The records Vyktor destroyed contained the names of informants. Publishing those names would have destroyed lives — Vyktor is right about that. His crime was not protecting murderers. His crime was deciding alone. The punishment for that is the end of his career in government, not a prison cell. There is a difference between justice and vengeance. I am trying to find it."

"Maren, close the investigation. Vyktor made a decision under extraordinary circumstances — the kind of decision no one should have to make, in a transition that no one had prepared for. He destroyed records that would have named informants, triggered reprisals, and destabilized the country at the moment it was most fragile. That is not obstruction of justice. That is what governing looks like in the space between a dictatorship and a democracy. I am not prosecuting my Chief of Staff for making a judgment call in a crisis that he did not create. The BCA's work has been invaluable. It is also complete. The cases you have already built can proceed. The Vyktor Reznik case does not."
